Why Your Stakeholder Engagement Plan Is Missing the Point

The most accurate message can fail when its audience does not trust the messenger.

Pupsi Phull · Phull Insights22 September 20262 min readLeadership & Transformation
Evidence boundary

Personal analysis and professional reflection based on earlier postgraduate work. Named-company examples describe historical research, not current 2026 corporate policies, figures or commitments. No unpublished case result is represented as a verified outcome.

Why this matters

Operational leaders often treat resistance as a communications failure: provide more data, repeat the rationale, and make the presentation clearer. But opposition to a facility, policy or technology can be rooted in trust and lived experience rather than a lack of information.

What the evidence suggests

Risk perception is influenced by what people have recently seen, how a proposal is framed, and who is speaking. A communication plan that counts meetings and messages but does not listen for these drivers can look busy while leaving the central concern untouched.

What it looks like in practice

In the historical risk-communication exercise behind this article, the useful question was not simply what to say. It was whose concerns had been heard, which claims could be independently checked, and whether feedback would change the decision process.

Practical next steps

Three things leaders can do now

01

Interview affected groups before drafting the message, and record the concern in their own words.

02

Separate technical evidence from the question of whether the source is trusted.

03

Track how concerns change after engagement, not just how many people attended.

Phull Insights Perspective

The view beneath the headline.

Being right is not the same as being heard. The best starting point is a perception and trust diagnosis, followed by clear evidence and a visible response to what people raise.

  • stakeholder engagement
  • risk perception
